paras: There is a sentence about learning that appears in roughly eleven thousand places online. It is short, it is memorable, and it is attributed, everywhere, to the same physicist. Teachers put it on classroom walls. It has been printed on a coffee mug since at least 2011. According to a researcher at a Dutch university who spent two years trying to verify it, the physicist never said it.

What he did say, in a lecture in 1953, was longer, slower and considerably less quotable. A journalist summarized it in a newspaper piece the following week — accurately, and in his own words, which is what a paraphrase is. Two months later a second paper reprinted the paraphrase inside quotation marks. From that point the sentence travelled on its own. Nobody had to misquote anybody deliberately. One set of punctuation marks did all the work.

This is why serious newsrooms keep a rule that sounds excessive until you understand it: a quotation is not verified by finding it in three places. It is verified by finding the original. Three places prove only that the sentence is popular. “People assume that if a claim is repeated it has been checked,” the researcher says. “Almost always, what has been checked is the previous copy. And the more confidently a sentence is asserted, the less often anybody asks where it came from.”

The uncomfortable part is the ending. When he published his findings, several teachers wrote to him and said, in effect, that they would go on using it. One of them put it differently, and better than the others: the sentence, she wrote, is truer than the thing the physicist actually said, and she was not going to take his word for it over her own thirty years in a classroom. He does not agree with her. He also admits that he cannot contradict her, because that is an argument about teaching and not about sourcing, and sourcing is the only thing he ever claimed.
reading.source: A composite account of a real class of error, written for this lesson. The physicist, the lecture and the researcher are invented.

choices: To warn readers that most famous quotations are invented.
To show how an honest paraphrase becomes a false quotation with nobody lying, and to end on somebody who keeps using it anyway.
To argue that teachers should not put quotations on classroom walls.

tips: He said that he had never said it.
Past simple steps back to past perfect.

items.situation: Report this question: “What do you want to do after the exam?”
tips: She asked me what I wanted to do after the exam.
No do, no inversion, no question mark. Normal word order.

items.situation: Report this order: “Submit the form before Friday.”
tips: They told me to submit the form before Friday.
Tell plus person plus to plus verb.

items.situation: Correct this out loud: He said me that he was tired.
tips: He told me that he was tired.
Tell takes a person directly. Say does not.

items.situation: Report something your cursinho teacher said this week.
tips: She explained that the second day was harder than the first.
Use a verb other than said. Explained, warned, pointed out.

items.situation: Now report a question somebody asked you this week, and your answer.
tips: He asked me whether I had finished the biology unit, and I told him I had not.
Whether for a yes or no question, and the answer steps back too.

listenings.text: The thing I was least prepared for was not the language. It was how much of the work is talking. In my first semester I was asked to defend a position in front of fourteen people, in week two, and nobody had warned me. Back home I had always been evaluated on what I wrote. Here I am evaluated on what I say, and on how quickly I can say it. My advice to anybody coming over is boring but I will give it anyway. Do not spend the last six months polishing your grammar. Spend them arguing out loud with somebody who disagrees with you, in English, about something you actually care about. That is the skill. The grammar arrives on its own if you use it enough.

We ran the oldest experiment in the book, the one children play at parties, but with adults and with a written text. Twelve people, each one reading the previous version once and then writing it from memory. What survives is not what you would guess. Numbers go first, almost immediately. Names go second. What survives to the twelfth person is the shape of the story and, above all, anything that sounds like a moral. In four of our five chains the twelfth version contained a sentence that appeared in none of the first eleven, and in every case it was the sentence that explained the point. People do not just lose information. They add the ending it should have had. That is not dishonesty. That is what memory is for.
